title: Repeating patterns: what comes next?

summary.text: Red, blue, red, blue, red. What comes next? You know before you see it. How? You will guess beans before they are put down, clap patterns, hunt for patterns at home and make a thoranam for your door. You will learn to find the part that repeats, carry a pattern on and spot a wrong piece. You will also find out that clap, stamp, clap, stamp and red, blue, red, blue are the same pattern.
summary.art: A girl on a kitchen floor guessing with one finger raised while her mother holds a bean hidden in her fist above a row of rajma and chana that take turns.

intro.hook: What comes next: red or blue?
intro.text: Blue comes next. Red and blue are taking turns, and it is blue's turn. You knew that without seeing the next bead. That is what a pattern does: it tells you what is coming. In this unit you will test how much of a row you need to see before you can know the rest.
intro.art: A string of big red and blue beads taking turns, with the next bead hidden inside a closed hand.

outcomes: I can spot a repeating pattern and say what repeats.
I can say what comes next in a pattern, and how I know.
I can find the part that repeats and say how long it is.
I can copy a pattern, carry it on and make my own.
I can make the same pattern with different things: colours, shapes, sounds and movements.
I can find a wrong piece or a missing piece in a pattern.

terms.meaning: Things set out by a rule, so that you can tell what comes next.
terms.example: Red, blue, red, blue is a pattern. You can tell that red comes next.
terms.art: A row of red and blue beads taking turns, with an arrow pointing to an empty space at the end.

terms.meaning: To do the same thing again.
terms.example: You clap, then you clap again. You have repeated the clap.
terms.art: Two pictures of the same pair of clapping hands, side by side.

terms.meaning: A pattern where one small part comes again and again, in the same order.
terms.example: Leaf, flower, leaf, flower, leaf, flower. The part leaf, flower comes three times.
terms.art: A string of mango leaves and marigolds taking turns across the top of a door.

terms.meaning: The smallest group of things that makes the whole pattern when you do it again and again. Grown-ups also call it the unit of repeat.
terms.example: In red, red, blue, red, red, blue, the part that repeats is red, red, blue. It is 3 long.
terms.art: A row of six beads, red, red, blue, red, red, blue, with a loop drawn round the first three.

terms.meaning: What the maker of a pattern follows. It tells you which thing comes next.
terms.example: The rule 'leaf, leaf, flower, then start again' makes the row leaf, leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, flower.
terms.art: A small card showing leaf, leaf, flower, held above a longer row made from it.

terms.meaning: To add more things to a pattern, keeping the same rule.
terms.example: The row is clap, stamp, clap, stamp. You carry it on with clap, stamp.
terms.art: A child adding two more beads to the end of a row that takes turns.

terms.meaning: One count in music. Beats come one after another at a steady speed, like footsteps.
terms.example: When you clap along to a song, each clap is on a beat.
terms.art: A child clapping while four evenly spaced dots run along a line under her.

terms.meaning: A repeating pattern of beats in Indian music. Singers keep it with claps, waves and finger counts.
terms.example: One way to keep the tala called Rupaka is clap, clap, wave, again and again.
terms.art: A singer sitting cross-legged, one hand clapping on her knee, then the same hand turned palm up in a wave.

terms.meaning: A string of leaves and flowers hung across the top of a door on festival days. It is also called a toran.
terms.example: A thoranam of mango leaves and marigolds: leaf, flower, leaf, flower.
terms.art: A doorway with a string of green mango leaves and orange marigolds hanging across the top.

terms.meaning: A strip along the edge of something, often filled with a pattern.
terms.example: The border of a sari has the same small shape again and again, all the way along.
terms.art: The edge of a silk sari with one small temple shape repeated along it.

explanations.context: This card says what a repeating pattern is. You met one in Guess My Next Bean, when the beans took turns.
explanations.definition: A repeating pattern is a row of things where one small part comes again and again, in the same order.
explanations.description: Look at the row: red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. The part red, blue comes three times. Nothing else is in the row. That makes it a repeating pattern. A pattern does not have to be colours. It can be shapes, sounds, movements or days. Clap, stamp, clap, stamp is a repeating pattern. So is day, night, day, night. A row with no part that comes again is not a repeating pattern. Red, blue, green, yellow, pink has five colours and no repeat.
examples: Leaf, flower, leaf, flower on a thoranam.
Black, yellow, black, yellow on the kerb stones along a road.
Tick, tock, tick, tock from a wall clock.
explanations.art: Six beads in a row, red and blue taking turns, with three loops drawn round the three red and blue pairs.

chart.title: Red, blue comes three times

explanations.context: This card shows how to find the part that repeats in a pattern. Once you have it, you know the whole pattern.
explanations.definition: The part that repeats is the smallest group of things that makes the whole pattern when you do it again and again.
explanations.description: Here is how to find it. Say the row aloud: red, red, blue, red, red, blue. Listen for where it starts again. It starts again after the blue. So the part that repeats is red, red, blue. It is 3 things long. Now check. Cover the first part with your hand. The rest of the row should begin in the same way. Always look for the smallest part. In a long red and blue row, red, blue, red, blue also comes again. But the smaller part, red, blue, already makes the whole row.
examples: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp: the part is clap, stamp. It is 2 long.
Leaf, leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, flower: the part is leaf, leaf, flower. It is 3 long.
Monday to Sunday, then Monday again: the part is 7 days long.
explanations.art: A child's hand covering the first three beads of a row, with the next three beads showing the same red, red, blue.

chart.title: The part is red, red, blue. It is 3 long.

explanations.concept: How to work out what comes next
explanations.context: This card shows, step by step, how to find the next thing in a pattern. It uses a thoranam of leaves and flowers.
explanations.definition: To find what comes next, find the part that repeats. Then see how far into the part the row has got.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The row is leaf, leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, flower, leaf. Step 1: find the part that repeats. It is leaf, leaf, flower. Step 2: look at the end of the row. After the last flower there is one leaf. So the row is one step into a new part. Step 3: the second thing in the part is a leaf. So a leaf comes next, and after it a flower. A common slip is to look only at the last thing. The last thing is a leaf. But in this pattern a leaf is sometimes followed by a leaf and sometimes by a flower. You need the whole part to know.
examples: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp, clap: the part is clap, stamp, so stamp comes next.
Red, blue, blue, red, blue: the part is red, blue, blue, so blue comes next.
Idli, idli, vada, idli, idli, vada: the part has ended, so it starts again with idli.
explanations.art: A thoranam with leaf, leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, flower, leaf on a string, and a child holding up a leaf and a flower, choosing.

chart.title: Leaf, leaf, flower. What comes next?

explanations.concept: The same pattern in different things
explanations.context: In One Pattern, Four Ways you made one pattern with sounds, beans, shapes and your body. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: Two rows are the same pattern when their things take turns in the same way, even if the things are different.
explanations.description: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp. Red, blue, red, blue. Circle, triangle, circle, triangle. Stand, squat, stand, squat. All four go like this: one thing, another thing, the first thing again, the other thing again. To check, do two of them together. Each time you clap, point at a red bead. Each time you stamp, point at a blue bead. If you reach the end without getting stuck, they are the same pattern. Grown-ups name patterns with letters. They call the first thing A and the second thing B. So all four rows are AB patterns. Clap, clap, stamp is an AAB pattern. Clap, stamp, pat is an ABC pattern.
examples: Tick, tock, tick, tock and left foot, right foot, left foot, right foot are both AB patterns.
Rajma, rajma, chana and clap, clap, wave are both AAB patterns.
Red, blue, yellow and ta, ka, di have three different things each. Both are ABC patterns.
explanations.art: Four rows one above the other: clapping hands and feet, red and blue beads, circles and triangles, and a child standing and squatting, all lined up in columns.

chart.title: Four rows, one pattern

explanations.concept: A part can have the same thing twice
explanations.context: This card is about patterns like red, red, blue. In the bean test, the row rajma, rajma, chana was one of these.
explanations.definition: A part that repeats can have the same thing in it twice. Red, red, blue is a different pattern from red, blue.
explanations.description: In a red, blue pattern, the colour changes every time. In a red, red, blue pattern, it does not. Red comes twice, then blue comes once. What tells the two patterns apart is the part that repeats. Red, blue is 2 long. Red, red, blue is 3 long. Red, blue, blue is also 3 long. But it is a third pattern, because now blue is the one that comes twice. Patterns like these often catch people out at the second bead. They expect a change, and the same bean comes again.
examples: Clap, clap, wave: the clap comes twice.
Idli, idli, vada on a plate, again and again.
Step, step, hop: two steps and then one hop.
explanations.art: Three short rows of beads one above the other: red and blue taking turns, then red, red, blue, then red, blue, blue.

chart.title: Three different patterns

explanations.concept: Finding a wrong piece or a missing piece
explanations.context: This card shows, step by step, how to find a piece that does not belong in a pattern. You do this in the game Pattern Train.
explanations.definition: A wrong piece is one that does not fit the part that repeats. You find it by saying the part again and again along the row.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The row is red, blue, red, blue, blue, blue. Step 1: find the part from the start of the row. It is red, blue. Step 2: touch each bead and say the part over and over: red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. Step 3: stop where your word and the bead do not match. At place 5 you say red, but the bead is blue. Place 5 has the wrong piece. A missing piece is found in the same way. Say the part along the row. The word you say at the gap is the missing piece.
examples: Leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, leaf, flower: place 4 should be a flower.
Clap, stamp, clap, (gap), clap, stamp: the gap should be a stamp.
Tick, tock, tick, tick: the last sound should be tock.
explanations.art: A finger touching the fifth bead of a row, red, blue, red, blue, blue, blue, with a speech bubble saying 'red?'.

chart.title: Say red, blue along the row. Where does it stop matching?

explanations.concept: Patterns in time: day and night, the week, the year
explanations.context: This card is about patterns you cannot hold in your hand, because they happen in time. Day and night is the biggest one you know.
explanations.definition: A pattern in time is something that happens again and again, in the same order.
explanations.description: Day, night, day, night is a repeating pattern. It happens because the Earth is a ball that spins. One full spin takes about 24 hours. When your side of the Earth faces the Sun, it is day. When your side faces away, it is night. The days of the week are a pattern with a part 7 long: Monday to Sunday, then Monday again. People chose to have 7 days in a week. The Earth did not choose it. The year is a pattern too. The Earth goes once round the Sun in about 365 days. So the hot months and the rains come back every year. These patterns are not perfectly even. The light part of the day is a little longer in summer than in winter. We still call each one a day.
examples: Your heart: lub, dub, lub, dub.
Your breath: in, out, in, out.
Breakfast, lunch, dinner, then breakfast again.
explanations.art: The Earth as a ball, half lit by the Sun and half dark, with a small arrow showing it spinning and a tiny house passing from the lit side to the dark side.

chart.title: One spin of the Earth

rows.label: half the Earth has day, half has night

explanations.concept: Other living beings make patterns too
explanations.context: People are not the only ones who make repeating patterns. This card tells you about two birds, an insect and a plant who do.
explanations.definition: Many living beings make repeating patterns with their voices, their lights and their bodies.
explanations.description: A coppersmith barbet is a small green bird with a red forehead, who lives in many Indian towns. They call tuk, tuk, tuk at a steady speed, about two tuks each second. One call can go on for as many as two hundred tuks. A common hawk-cuckoo, also called the brainfever bird, sings a call of three notes. They repeat it five or six times, louder each time, and then stop suddenly. Fireflies make patterns with light. Each kind of firefly flashes in a pattern of their own. That is how fireflies of one kind find each other in the dark. Plants make patterns as they grow. A rice plant or a maize plant puts out one leaf on one side, the next leaf on the other side, and so on up the stem: left, right, left, right.
examples: A barbet's call: tuk, tuk, tuk, tuk.
A hawk-cuckoo's call: three notes, then the same three notes again, louder.
A maize plant's leaves: left, right, left, right.

perspectives.explanation: The barbet keeps a steady beat for minutes at a time, as a drummer does. Other barbets hear the call and know who is there.
They say the call is an automatic habit of the bird's body, and that the bird is not making a pattern on purpose.

explanations.art: A small green bird with a red forehead on a bare branch, beak open, with a row of evenly spaced marks labelled tuk, tuk, tuk coming from the beak.

chart.title: The barbet's call, three seconds of it

explanations.concept: Can you ever be sure what comes next?
explanations.context: This card asks an honest question about every 'what comes next?' puzzle. It is about who decides the answer.
explanations.definition: A few beads can fit more than one rule. The maker of the pattern is the one who knows the rule.
explanations.description: You see red, blue, red, blue. What comes next? Almost everyone says red. That is the best guess. The simplest rule that fits is red, blue, again and again. But another rule also fits what you have seen: red, blue, red, blue, green, and then all five again. With that rule, green comes next. So a few beads fit more than one rule. Only the maker knows which rule she is using. The more of the row you see, the safer your guess becomes. In school questions, people agree to pick the simplest rule.
examples: Red, blue, red, blue, then green: the part could be 5 long.
Idli on Monday, dosa on Tuesday, idli on Wednesday. Will Thursday be dosa? Only the cook knows.

perspectives.explanation: There is one right answer. Find the smallest part that repeats and carry it on.
Any rule that fits the beads you have seen is allowed. Picking the simplest rule is a sensible habit that people agreed on. It is not a law.

explanations.art: A row of red, blue, red, blue beads and two thought bubbles above the empty next place, one with a red bead and one with a green bead.

chart.title: Red? Or something else?

agreed.text: Once you know the part that repeats, you can say what comes next without seeing it.
agreed.evidence: In Guess My Next Bean, the crosses come at the start of each row. After the part has come round twice, careful guessers get every bean right.

agreed.text: The same pattern can be made with sounds, colours, shapes or movements.
agreed.evidence: In One Pattern, Four Ways, you clap and stamp while pointing along a row of beans. Every clap lands on one kind of bean and every stamp on the other, with nothing left over.

agreed.text: Day and night take turns because the Earth spins.
agreed.evidence: Astronauts and satellites watch the Earth turn. One full turn takes about 24 hours. As the Earth turns, the line between day and night moves across the land.

agreed.text: Small children who are good with patterns tend to do well in maths when they are older.
agreed.evidence: Researchers in the USA followed 517 children from age 4 to age 11. How well a child did with patterns at age 4 helped to predict that child's maths marks in Class 5 (Rittle-Johnson and others, 2017). This does not prove that playing with patterns causes the better marks.

challenging.claim: If a row goes red, blue, red, blue, the next bead must be red.
challenging.context: This card looks at a claim that sounds certain. It asks whether a few beads are enough to be sure.
challenging.for: Red is the simplest way to carry the row on. It is the answer nearly everyone expects.
challenging.against: Four beads fit more than one rule. The maker could be using red, blue, red, blue, green. Red is the best guess, but only the maker knows the rule.

challenging.claim: Patterns are only for decoration. They are not real maths.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that borders and bead rows are art work, and maths begins with numbers.
challenging.for: Borders, rangoli and thoranams are made to look good. Nobody needs numbers to enjoy them.
challenging.against: The English mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote in 1940 that a mathematician is 'a maker of patterns'. Finding the part that repeats, and using it to say what comes next, is the same thinking a child later uses in times tables and algebra.

challenging.claim: Nothing ever really repeats, because no two things are exactly the same.
challenging.who: An idea that follows from Heraclitus, a Greek thinker of about 2,500 years ago, who said that everything keeps changing
challenging.context: This card asks whether a repeat is ever a true repeat. It matters, because every pattern is built from repeats.
challenging.for: No two marigolds are the same size. No two claps are equally loud. Today is not the same as yesterday.
challenging.against: A pattern does not need its things to be exactly alike. It needs us to agree what counts as the same: any marigold is a flower, any clap is a clap. With that agreement, a pattern tells us what comes next, and the guess comes true.

big_questions.q: How many beads do you need to see before you can call a row a pattern?
big_questions.hint: Is one red and one blue enough? What about red, blue, red?

big_questions.q: Is clap, clap, clap, clap a pattern? What is the part that repeats?
big_questions.hint: Can a part be just one thing?

big_questions.q: Can two people look at the same row and find different parts that repeat?
big_questions.hint: Look at blue, red, blue, red, blue, red. Now cover the first bead. What does the row look like?

big_questions.q: Why does it feel good to know what comes next?
big_questions.hint: Think of a song you know well, or a story you have heard many times.

big_questions.q: What would life be like if day and night did not take turns?
big_questions.hint: When would you sleep? When would the birds sing?

big_questions.q: Does a barbet know they are making a pattern?
big_questions.hint: How could you find out? What would you watch for?

roots.context: We guessed beans, clapped, hunted for patterns and made a thoranam. Now let us think about what a pattern really is.

deep_truth.truth: In One Pattern, Four Ways, you clapped and stamped, then laid rajma and chana in the same way. A clap is nothing like a bean. Still, you called them the same pattern. So a pattern is not the things. It is the way the things take turns.
deep_truth.habit: We think a pattern is made of its things: these colours, these beads. But you can swap every thing for another, and the pattern is still there. And we are the ones who say the two rows are the same.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Pattern, Four Ways, one pattern was made with claps, beans, drawn shapes and your body. In Guess My Next Bean, you knew the next bean from the turns, before you saw it.

three.who_am_i: Your heart goes lub, dub, lub, dub. Your feet go left, right, left, right. You are full of patterns. You are also the one who notices them.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings make patterns. A coppersmith barbet calls tuk, tuk, tuk. A rice plant puts out leaves left, right, left, right.
three.what_is_this_world: Day follows night again and again, because the Earth keeps turning. But no two days are exactly alike. We choose to call each one a day.

roots.thread: Start with one thing: a clap. Do it again, and now there is a repeat. Put a stamp in between, and there is a pattern. From that one small part, a row can go on as long as you like. A long thoranam, a whole song and a year of days all grow from one small part, done again and again.

teachings.teaching: The Gita says that the whole crowd of living beings comes out when Brahma's day begins and melts away when the night comes, again and again.
teachings.link: This is day and night seen as one huge repeating pattern. The same part, day and then night, comes round again and again.

teachings.teaching: This old Hebrew book says that the sun rises and the sun goes down, and hurries back to the place where it rises.
teachings.link: People far from India watched the same pattern in the sky long ago, and wrote it down.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, as reported by Plato in Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, said that you could not step twice into the same river, because the water keeps flowing.
teachings.link: This is the other side of every pattern. No two claps and no two days are exactly alike. To see a pattern, we agree to treat them as the same.

science.text: Small children can copy a row of beads, and carry it on, before they can make the same pattern with new things. Researchers in the USA found this with 4-year-olds (Rittle-Johnson and others, 2013). Seeing that the pattern is not the things is the harder step.
Is a pattern out in the world, or in the mind that notices it? Thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.view: They say patterns are in the world, whether or not anyone notices them. Day and night took turns for a very long time before there were any people to call it a pattern. The Earth turns the same way with nobody watching. They say we do not decide which things are the same. We find out.

practice.title: Listen to your own pattern
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Put one hand on your chest. Feel your heart beat, again and again. Now feel your breath go in and out, in and out. Stay with it for ten breaths. Then open your eyes. Which was faster, your heart or your breath? Was every breath exactly the same?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put a hand on your chest. Feel your heart beat. Feel your breath go in and out. Count ten breaths. Was every breath the same?

ask: Is the pattern in the beads, or in the one who looks at them?
If nobody heard the barbet, would tuk, tuk, tuk still be a pattern?
No two days are exactly alike. Why do we still say that day and night repeat?
Can something happen only once and still be a pattern?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed and one hand on her chest, with a thoranam of leaves and flowers over the door behind her and a small green bird on the window bar.

how_we_found_out.context: How do we know what it takes to understand a pattern? This card tells the true story of three researchers who tested children just before they started school.
how_we_found_out.story: For many years, teachers gave small children rows of beads to copy and carry on. If a child got the beads right, people thought the child understood the pattern. Three researchers in Australia, Marina Papic, Joanne Mulligan and Michael Mitchelmore, tested this. They worked with 53 children from two preschools, in the year before the children started school. They asked each child to copy patterns, carry them on and talk about them. Many children saw a row only as things taking turns: red, then blue, then red. They did not see that one small part was being repeated. In one of the preschools, the teachers then spent six months helping children to find that part. Afterwards those children did much better on pattern tasks than the children at the other preschool. They were still ahead a year later, after their first year at school. The study came out in 2011.
how_we_found_out.who: Marina Papic, Joanne Mulligan and Michael Mitchelmore
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A child who can carry on a row of beads understands the pattern. The 2011 study showed this was wrong. Many children carried rows on by treating them as things taking turns, without seeing the part that repeats.

story.title: Tak, Tak, Tok
story.note: Yazhini, Kabilan and Selvi akka are made up, and so is this three-strike step. Kolattam is a real stick dance from Tamil Nadu. It is danced with two sticks, often at Pongal and Navaratri.
text: Yazhini was eight, and this year she was in the kolattam line.
Kolattam is a dance with sticks. Each dancer holds two short wooden sticks, one in each hand. The dancers stand in two rows, each facing a partner, and strike their sticks in time with a song.
The dance was for Pongal evening, at the end of their street in Thanjavur. There were four days left.
Her cousin Kabilan was six. He had come from Tiruchi for the holidays, and he wanted to dance too.
"He is small," said Selvi akka, who taught the dance. "But there is a gap in the line, right across from you. If he can learn the step by Thursday, he is in."
The singer began. The sticks began. Tak, tak, tok. Tak, tak, tok.
Kabilan fixed his eyes on Yazhini's hands. When her sticks tapped each other, he tapped his. When her right stick came across, he sent his own across to meet it.
But he was always a little late. By the time he tapped his sticks together, she was already reaching over. Her stick met his fingers.
"Ow!"
"Sorry! Again."
Tak, tak. "Ow!"
On the second day it was the same. Kabilan watched harder. He watched so hard that he forgot to blink. The harder he watched, the later he was.
On the third day Selvi akka looked at his red knuckles and sighed. "Maybe next year, kanna."
Kabilan sat down on the temple step with his sticks across his knees. He did not cry, but only just.
Yazhini sat down next to him. She was hot and cross. She wanted a partner, and she did not want to tell him to go home.
How do I do it? she wondered. I never look at anyone's hands. So how do I know when to reach across?
She tried to catch herself knowing it. She could not. So she shut her eyes and listened to the others, who were still dancing.
Tak, tak, tok. Tak, tak, tok. Tak, tak, tok.
It was only three sounds. The same three, over and over. Nobody out there was dancing a long dance. They were dancing a very short one, again and again.
"Kabilan," she said. "Stop looking at me."
"Then how will I know what you are doing?"
"You already know. Close your eyes. Say it with me. Mine, mine, yours."
"Mine, mine, yours," said Kabilan.
"Again. Do not stop."
"Mine, mine, yours. Mine, mine, yours. Mine, mine, yours." His fingers began to tap on the step all by themselves. Two small taps, one big one.
"Now tell me. After mine, mine, what comes?"
"Yours."
"Do you need to see me move first?"
Kabilan opened his eyes. He thought about it. "No," he said slowly. "It is always yours."
They stood up. "Look at my nose, not my hands," said Yazhini. "And keep saying it."
Mine, mine. Their sticks came across at the very same moment and met in the middle. Tok! It was a clean, loud tok, the best one all week.
Mine, mine, tok. Mine, mine, tok. On the fourth time round, Kabilan grinned so widely that he lost his place and hit the air.
"Start the part again," said Yazhini. "It is always the same part."

On Pongal evening there was a kolam at every door, and mango leaves strung over every doorway. The singer sang faster and faster towards the end, the way she always did. Kabilan's lips moved. Mine, mine, yours. He did not look at Yazhini's hands once. The last tok rang out, and Selvi akka nodded at him from the side.
They walked home in the dark. Kabilan ran one stick along a gate. Tak, tak, tak.
"Akka, look," he said. "The street lights. Light, dark, light, dark."
"Mm."
"And the kerb. Black, yellow, black, yellow. And listen, somebody's cooker is whistling. Whistle, wait, whistle, wait."
"Now you will never stop," said Yazhini.
Kabilan pointed his stick down the long street, at the next light, and the dark after it, and the light after that.
"I know what comes next," he said. And he did.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kabilan fails while he copies one move at a time, because a copy always comes late. He gets it when he hears the small part that repeats: mine, mine, yours. Then he knows the next move before it comes. Knowing a pattern means knowing what comes next without being shown.
ask: Why was Kabilan always late when he watched Yazhini's hands?
What was the part that repeated in the dance?
How did saying 'mine, mine, yours' help Kabilan?
On the walk home, Kabilan found patterns everywhere. Which patterns can you find on your street?

experiments.title: Guess My Next Bean: when can you know what is coming?
experiments.context: In this test a grown-up builds three rows of beans, one bean at a time. You guess each bean before it is put down. A right guess gets a tick and a wrong guess gets a cross. The point is to find out when your guesses stop being luck.
experiments.question: How many beans do you need to see before you can say what comes next, every time?
experiments.predict: Before each row, guess: will this row be easy or hard to guess? Why do you think so? Then, before every bean, guess which kind it will be.
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up chooses each row's rule before starting and does not change it halfway. The child guesses before every bean, even the first ones. Every guess gets a tick or a cross, so no guess is forgotten.
results_table: A tick or a cross under each bean
The bean number of my last cross

materials.item: white chana (kabuli chana), or any bean of another colour
a bowl to keep the grown-up's beans in
two sheets of paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep beans and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Guess three rows of beans, one bean at a time. Mark ticks and crosses. Then make a row of your own for the grown-up to guess.

experiments.record: The beans are laid on paper, and a tick or a cross is written under each one. In a table, write what took turns in each row and the bean number of the last cross. Under the table, a grown-up writes what the child found, in the child's own words.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your guesses and crosses will be your own)

setup.art: A grown-up and a child sitting on the floor with a sheet of paper between them, the grown-up holding a small bowl of rajma, chana and buttons close to her chest.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up keeps the beans. The child sits facing the paper.

setup.art: A row of four beans on the paper with a pencilled tick or cross under each, and the grown-up's closed fist held above the next empty place while the child points and guesses.
setup.caption: 2. Guess the next bean. Then the grown-up puts it down.

setup.art: A finished row of twelve beans with two crosses under the first beans and ten ticks under the rest.
setup.caption: 3. A tick for a right guess, a cross for a wrong one. Look where the crosses are.

flow.do: 1. Keep the beans in a bowl on your side. 2. Say you will make a row, one bean at a time. 3. Before each bean, your child guesses which kind it will be. 4. Put the bean down on the paper. Write a tick or a cross under it. 5. Row 1 is rajma, chana, rajma, chana, up to 12 beans.
flow.say: I am making a row of beans. Before I put each one down, guess which bean it will be.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a row, one bean at a time. Guess each bean before you see it. A right guess gets a tick.
flow.parent: Do not say the word 'pattern' yet. The first guess or two can only be luck. That is fine. Keep a straight face and keep the same speed for every bean.

chart.title: How one row is marked

flow.context: This is the first step of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you guess row 1.

flow.do: 1. Look at the ticks and crosses together. 2. Ask where the crosses are. 3. Ask how your child knew the later beans. 4. Just listen. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Look at your ticks and crosses. Where are the crosses? How did you know the later beans?
flow.kid: Look at your ticks and crosses. Where are the crosses? How did you know the later beans?

ask.q: How did you know what was coming?
good: They take turns.
It goes rajma, chana, rajma, chana.
It keeps doing the same thing.

flow.parent: Most children get a cross or two at the start, and then all ticks. Whatever your child's sheet shows, ask about it. Do not correct it.

chart.title: The first six beans of row 1 can look like this

flow.context: This is step 2 of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you look at the ticks and crosses for row 1.

flow.do: 1. Clear the paper. Show a rajma, a chana and a button. 2. Ask if this row will be easier or harder, and why. 3. Write the guess. 4. Row 2 is rajma, chana, button, then the same again, up to 12. 5. Your child guesses every bean. Mark ticks and crosses.
flow.say: This time I will use three kinds. Will this row be easier or harder to guess? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now there are three kinds. Will it be easier or harder? Say why. Then guess each bean.
flow.parent: Many children guess rajma for the third bean, because row 1 went back to rajma. The button is a surprise. Let it be one.

chart.title: Row 2 uses three kinds

flow.context: This is step 3 of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you guess row 2, which has three kinds of thing.

flow.do: 1. Clear the paper. Put the buttons away. 2. Ask if this row will be easier or harder than the button row, and why. 3. Row 3 is rajma, rajma, chana, then the same again, up to 12. 4. Your child guesses every bean. Mark ticks and crosses.
flow.say: Now only rajma and chana again. Will it be easier or harder than the button row? Why?
flow.kid: Only rajma and chana now. Will it be easy or hard? Say why. Then guess each bean.
flow.parent: The second rajma is the surprise in this row. Children who expect a change every time get crosses at beans 2 and 3. Some get one more cross at bean 5.

check.q: A row goes rajma, rajma, chana, rajma, rajma, chana, rajma. What comes next?
check.why: Rajma comes next. The part that repeats is rajma, rajma, chana. The row has just begun a new part with one rajma, so the second rajma follows. Picking chana means expecting the two kinds to take turns one by one.

chart.title: Row 3 uses two kinds

flow.context: This is step 4 of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you guess row 3, which has two kinds again but a new rule.

flow.do: 1. Find the last cross in each row. 2. Write its bean number in the table. 3. Ask which row had crosses for the longest, and why.
flow.say: Find your last cross in each row. Which row took you the longest to work out? Why?
flow.kid: Find your last cross in each row. Which row took the longest to work out?

ask.q: Why did that row take longer to work out?
good: Three things took turns, not two.
Rajma came twice, and I did not expect it.
I had to see more beans before I knew.

chart.title: One family's table (yours will be your own)

flow.context: This is step 5 of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you compare the three rows.

flow.do: 1. Swap places. Give your child the bowl. 2. Your child makes a secret row for you. 3. Guess each bean aloud before it is put down. 4. Guess wrong once or twice at the start.
flow.say: Now you make a row for me. Choose what takes turns. Do not tell me.
flow.kid: Now you make the row. Choose what takes turns. Keep it the same all the way.
flow.parent: If your child's row stops repeating, do not call it wrong. Ask: 'Can I ever guess this right? What would help me?' Children usually see that the guesser needs the same part to come again.
flow.context: This is step 6 of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you make a secret row and the grown-up guesses.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child found out. 2. Ask what they saw that makes them think so. 3. Write their words under the table. 4. Only then give the name: a repeating pattern.
flow.say: What did you find out? Tell me what you saw. Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found out. Say what you saw. Say why you think so.

ask.q: When could you be sure of the next bean?
good: After it started again.
When I had seen the same part two times.
At the start I could only guess. Later I knew.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'At the start I could only guess. When the same part had come round two times, I knew every bean.' After your child has said it in their own words, you can say that a row like this is called a repeating pattern.
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess My Next Bean, a test where a grown-up builds a row one bean at a time and you guess each bean first. Here you say what you found.

activities.title: One Pattern, Four Ways
activities.context: In this activity you take one pattern and make it four ways: with sounds, with beans, with drawn shapes and with your body. The point is to find out whether a pattern can move from one kind of thing to another.
activities.problem: Can a sound pattern and a bean pattern be the same pattern?

schedule.what: Clap and stamp a pattern. Then make the same pattern with beans, with drawn shapes and with your body.

activities.record: Draw the four rows one under the other: the sounds, the beans, the shapes and the body moves. Line them up so that each clap sits above one bean and one shape.

setup.art: A parent and child standing face to face, both clapping, with one foot lifted ready to stamp.
setup.caption: 1. Clap, stamp, clap, stamp.

setup.art: A child laying rajma and chana in a row on the floor, one bean for each sound, while the parent claps.
setup.caption: 2. Make the same pattern with beans.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a row of circles and triangles taking turns, and beside it a child standing tall and then squatting.
setup.caption: 3. Make it again with shapes, then with your body.

flow.do: 1. Clap once, then stamp once. 2. Keep going: clap, stamp, clap, stamp. 3. Your child joins in. 4. Stop suddenly after a clap. Ask what comes next.
flow.say: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp. Join in. When I stop, tell me what comes next.
flow.kid: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp. Keep going. Stop after a clap. What comes next?

chart.title: Clap, stamp

flow.context: This is the first step of One Pattern, Four Ways, where you make one pattern with sounds, beans, shapes and your body. Here you make the pattern with sounds.

flow.do: 1. Put out the rajma and the chana. 2. Ask your child to make the clap and stamp pattern with beans. 3. Let your child choose which bean is the clap. 4. Clap and stamp slowly while your child points along the row.
flow.say: Now make the same pattern with beans. Which bean will be the clap? Which will be the stamp?
flow.kid: Make the same pattern with beans. Choose a bean for clap. Choose a bean for stamp.

ask.q: How did you decide which bean to put next?
good: Clap is rajma, so after rajma comes chana.
I said clap, stamp in my head.
They take turns like the sounds.

flow.parent: Some children lay all the rajma first and then all the chana. If so, clap and stamp slowly and ask them to point to a bean for each sound. They will find the row does not fit.

chart.title: One bean for each sound

flow.context: This is step 2 of One Pattern, Four Ways, where you make one pattern with sounds, beans, shapes and your body. Here you turn the sound pattern into a bean pattern.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the pattern with two shapes: a circle for clap and a triangle for stamp. 2. Then your child does it with the body: stand tall for clap, squat for stamp. 3. Do the body pattern together four times round.
flow.say: Now draw it. Use a circle for clap and a triangle for stamp. Then show me with your whole body.
flow.kid: Draw it: a circle for clap, a triangle for stamp. Then stand for clap and squat for stamp.

chart.title: Four ways so far

flow.context: This is step 3 of One Pattern, Four Ways, where you make one pattern with sounds, beans, shapes and your body. Here you make the pattern with shapes and then with your body.

flow.do: 1. Point to the bean row and clap once. 2. Ask whether the claps and the beans are the same pattern. 3. Ask what is the same about them. 4. Listen first. Then say the idea in one sentence.
flow.say: A clap is a sound. A bean is a thing. Are these two the same pattern? What is the same about them?
flow.kid: A clap is a sound. A bean is a thing. Are they the same pattern? What is the same?

ask.q: What is the same about the claps and the beans?
good: They both go one, the other, one, the other.
Two things take turns.
When I clap, I can point at a rajma every time.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, you can say it: the pattern is the way the things take turns. The things themselves can change.

check.q: Which bean row is the same pattern as clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap, stamp?
options: rajma, chana, rajma, chana, rajma, chana
rajma, rajma, chana, rajma, rajma, chana
rajma, chana, chana, rajma, chana, chana
check.why: Rajma, rajma, chana matches. Each clap is a rajma and each stamp is a chana: two the same, then one different. Picking the first row means matching the two kinds of thing, but not how many times each one comes.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Pattern, Four Ways, where you make one pattern with sounds, beans, shapes and your body. Here you decide whether the four rows are one pattern.

activities.title: Pattern Hunt at Home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and look for things that repeat: tiles, grills, stripes and borders. The point is to see that repeating patterns are all around you, and to tell them from things that do not repeat.
activities.problem: Which things in your home are repeating patterns, and which are not?

materials.item: paper and a pencil or crayons

schedule.what: Find three repeating patterns at home. Say each one aloud, find the part that repeats and draw it. Then find one thing that is not a repeating pattern.

activities.record: Draw three patterns you found. Draw a loop round the part that repeats in each one.

setup.art: A child crouching on a tiled floor, touching the tiles one after another, with a window grill and a striped towel on a chair behind her.
setup.caption: 1. Look for things that repeat: tiles, grills, stripes, borders.

setup.art: A child's finger moving along the bars of a window grill, with a speech bubble saying 'bar, gap, bar, gap'.
setup.caption: 2. Touch along it and say it aloud.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three small drawings of patterns, each with a pencil loop round one part.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it. Loop the part that repeats.

flow.do: 1. Walk round your home together. 2. Look at floors, window grills, towels, bedsheets, saris, shirts and railings. 3. Your child finds three things that repeat. 4. Write where each one was.
flow.say: Let us hunt for patterns. Find three things in our home that do the same thing again and again.
flow.kid: Walk round your home. Find three things that repeat. Look at tiles, grills, stripes and borders.
flow.parent: Good places to look: floor tiles, a window grill, a striped towel or shirt, the border of a sari, dupatta or bedsheet, a stack of bangles, the stairs.

chart.title: One family's hunt (yours will be your own)

flow.context: This is the first step of the Pattern Hunt, where you look for repeating patterns around your home. Here you find three patterns.

flow.do: 1. Go back to each pattern. 2. Your child touches along it and says it aloud. 3. Ask which part repeats and how long it is. 4. Your child draws the pattern and loops one part.
flow.say: Touch along it and say what you see. Which part comes again and again? How many things are in it?
flow.kid: Touch along each pattern. Say it aloud. Draw it. Loop the part that repeats.

ask.q: How long is the part that repeats?
good: Two: bar, gap.
Three: thin stripe, thin stripe, thick stripe.
It is one flower shape, then a dot.

chart.title: A window grill, said aloud

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Pattern Hunt, where you look for repeating patterns around your home. Here you find the part that repeats in each pattern you found.

flow.do: 1. Now find one thing that is not a repeating pattern. 2. Try the vegetable basket, a shelf of books or the things on a table. 3. Ask why it is not a repeating pattern. 4. Ask how it could be made into one.
flow.say: Now find something that is not a repeating pattern. How do you know it is not one?
flow.kid: Find one thing that is not a repeating pattern. Say why not.

ask.q: How could you turn it into a repeating pattern?
good: Line up the vegetables: tomato, onion, tomato, onion.
Put the books tall, short, tall, short.

check.q: Which of these is a repeating pattern?
options: Stripes on a towel: blue, white, blue, white
check.why: The towel stripes repeat: the part blue, white comes again and again. The vegetables and the clouds have no part that comes again in the same order. Picking them means calling anything with many things in it a pattern.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Pattern Hunt, where you look for repeating patterns around your home. Here you find something that does not repeat.

activities.title: Maths in life: a thoranam for your door
activities.context: In this activity you make a thoranam, the string of leaves and flowers that hangs over a door on festival days. You choose a repeating pattern, work out how many leaves and flowers you need, and string them in order. The point is to plan a pattern before you make it.
activities.problem: A thoranam looks right only if its pattern is kept all the way along. How do you plan it so that you cut the right number of each piece?

materials.item: green paper, or newspaper coloured green, for leaves
yellow or orange paper for flowers
string or thick thread, as long as your door is wide
if you have them: fresh mango leaves and marigolds, with a needle and thread for the grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with sharp scissors, and all the work with a needle.

schedule.what: Choose a pattern, count the pieces you need, cut them, lay them in order, tape them to a string and hang it over a door.

activities.record: Draw your thoranam. Write its rule under it, for example 'leaf, leaf, flower', and how many times the part comes.

setup.art: A child at a low table pointing at a small plan drawn on paper: leaf, flower, leaf, flower, with paper leaves and flowers in two heaps beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Choose your pattern. Count the pieces you need.

setup.art: Paper leaves and flowers laid in a long row on the floor in a repeating pattern, with a string lying along the top of the row.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the pieces in order before you stick them.

setup.art: A finished paper thoranam of green leaves and orange flowers taped across the top of a front door, with a child looking up at it.
setup.caption: 3. Tape them to the string and hang it over the door.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child what a thoranam is: a string of leaves and flowers over a door on festival days. 2. Your child chooses a pattern for it. 3. Your child says the rule aloud, three times round. 4. Draw the plan on paper.
flow.say: We will make a thoranam for our door. Choose a pattern of leaves and flowers. Say it to me.
flow.kid: Choose a pattern of leaves and flowers. Say it aloud three times round.
flow.parent: Leaf, flower is the simplest. Leaf, leaf, flower and leaf, flower, flower are good next choices. Let your child choose.

chart.title: One plan: leaf, flower

flow.context: This is the first step of the Door Thoranam, a string of paper leaves and flowers made in a repeating pattern. Here you choose the pattern.

flow.do: 1. Decide how many times the part will come. Four to six times fits most doors. 2. Ask how many leaves and how many flowers that needs. 3. Your child draws leaf and flower shapes about as long as a finger. 4. Cut them out.
flow.say: Your part will come six times. How many leaves do we need? How many flowers?
flow.kid: How many times will your part come? Count the leaves you need. Count the flowers. Draw them.

ask.q: Your pattern is leaf, leaf, flower and you want it 4 times. How many leaves must we cut?
good: Two leaves each time: 2, 4, 6, 8.

flow.parent: Let your child work it out by drawing the plan and counting, or by counting in twos. Do not give the number.

chart.title: For leaf, flower, six times

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Door Thoranam, a string of paper leaves and flowers made in a repeating pattern. Here you work out how many leaves and flowers to cut.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays all the pieces in a row on the floor, in order. 2. Your child reads the row aloud from one end to the other. 3. Fix any piece that is out of place. 4. Lay the string along the top and tape each piece to it.
flow.say: Lay all the pieces in order first. Read the row to me. Is every piece in the right place?
flow.kid: Lay the pieces in a row. Read the row aloud. Then tape each piece to the string.
flow.parent: Laying the row first lets your child find and fix a wrong piece before the tape goes on. If a piece is wrong, ask your child to read the row aloud again and listen for it.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Door Thoranam, a string of paper leaves and flowers made in a repeating pattern. Here you lay the pieces in order and fix them to the string.

flow.do: 1. Hang the thoranam across the top of a door. 2. Ask someone else at home to read the pattern aloud. 3. Ask them what would come next if it were longer.
flow.say: Ask someone to read your thoranam. Can they tell what would come next?
flow.kid: Hang it over a door. Ask someone to read it. Can they say what comes next?

check.q: A thoranam goes leaf, leaf, flower, leaf, leaf, flower, leaf. What are the next two pieces?
check.why: Leaf, then flower. The part that repeats is leaf, leaf, flower. The row has just begun a new part with one leaf, so a second leaf and then a flower follow. Picking 'flower, leaf' means thinking the leaf and the flower take turns one by one.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Door Thoranam, a string of paper leaves and flowers made in a repeating pattern. Here you hang it up and test it on someone.

activities.title: Maths in life: Ta Ka Di Mi, patterns you say and clap
activities.context: In this activity you say and clap the repeating patterns that South Indian musicians use to keep time. The point is to feel a pattern with your voice and hands, and to find the part that repeats by listening.
activities.problem: Musicians and dancers must all stay together. How does a repeating pattern of claps help them?

schedule.what: Say ta ka di mi and ta ki ta round and round with a clap on the first sound. Then keep clap, clap, wave.

activities.record: Draw the hand pattern clap, clap, wave three times round. Use a hand shape for a clap and a wavy line for a wave.

setup.art: A child and a parent sitting cross-legged facing each other, mouths open mid-syllable, each with one hand raised above the knee ready to clap.
setup.caption: 1. Say ta ka di mi round and round. Clap on every ta.

setup.art: The same two people, one hand clapping down on the knee and then the same hand turned palm up beside the knee.
setup.caption: 2. Clap, clap, wave: a wave is the hand turned palm up.

flow.do: 1. Sit facing each other. 2. Say ta ka di mi slowly and evenly, round and round. 3. Clap your hand on your knee on every ta. 4. Go round eight times. Then stop and ask what the part that repeats is.
flow.say: Say it with me: ta ka di mi, ta ka di mi. Clap on every ta. Do not stop.
flow.kid: Say ta ka di mi, round and round. Clap on every ta. Go round eight times.
flow.parent: Saying rhythm sounds like these is called solkattu. Carnatic drummers and dancers learn their patterns this way. Keep the speed steady, like slow footsteps.

chart.title: Four sounds. Clap on ta.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ta Ka Di Mi, where you say and clap the repeating patterns of South Indian music. Here you say a pattern of four sounds.

flow.do: 1. Change to ta ki ta, round and round. 2. Clap on the first ta each time. 3. Go round eight times. 4. Ask which pattern has the longer part: ta ka di mi or ta ki ta.
flow.say: Now a new one: ta ki ta, ta ki ta. Clap on the first ta. Which pattern has the longer part?
flow.kid: Now say ta ki ta, round and round. Clap on the first ta. Which part is longer?

ask.q: How many sounds are in the part ta ki ta? How many in ta ka di mi?
good: Three, and four.
Ta ka di mi is longer by one.

chart.title: Three sounds. Clap on the first ta.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Ta Ka Di Mi, where you say and clap the repeating patterns of South Indian music. Here you say a pattern of three sounds and compare it with the pattern of four.

flow.do: 1. Show a wave: turn your hand palm up beside your knee. 2. Keep clap, clap, wave, round and round, at a steady speed. 3. Your child joins in for eight rounds. 4. Ask which bean row from the bean test goes the same way.
flow.say: Carnatic singers keep time with their hands. Try this one: clap, clap, wave. Which bean row went the same way?
flow.kid: Clap, clap, wave. Keep going for eight rounds. Which bean row went the same way?

ask.q: Which bean row went like clap, clap, wave?
good: Rajma, rajma, chana.
The one where rajma came twice.

flow.parent: Many Carnatic students keep the tala called Rupaka in this way: two claps and a wave. If someone at home sings, ask them to show you.

check.q: Clap, clap, wave, clap, clap, wave. Which is the part that repeats?
check.why: The part is clap, clap, wave. It is 3 long, and the whole row is made by doing it again and again. Picking 'clap, wave' leaves out the second clap.

chart.title: Clap, clap, wave

flow.context: This is the last step of Ta Ka Di Mi, where you say and clap the repeating patterns of South Indian music. Here you keep a hand pattern that Carnatic singers use.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: who else makes patterns?
activities.context: In this activity you sit by a window and listen for sounds that repeat, made by birds, insects, people and machines. Then you write one sound pattern down with marks. The point is to notice that other beings make repeating patterns too.
activities.problem: Who and what around your home makes a repeating pattern of sound?

schedule.what: Listen at a window for three minutes. Pick one repeating sound and write it with marks. Then find out about the coppersmith barbet's call.

activities.record: Write one sound pattern with marks: a dot for a short sound, a line for a long sound and a gap for a silence. Write who or what made it.

setup.art: A child sitting by an open window with eyes closed and a hand cupped behind one ear, with a crow on a wire and a wall clock in view.
setup.caption: 1. Sit by a window. Close your eyes. Listen for three minutes.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a row of pencil dots and short lines taking turns, labelled 'clock'.
setup.caption: 2. Write one sound pattern with dots and lines.

flow.do: 1. Sit together by an open window or on a balcony. 2. Close your eyes for three minutes. 3. Each time you hear a sound that repeats, whisper what it is. 4. Afterwards, list the sounds.
flow.say: Close your eyes and listen. Tell me every sound that comes again and again.
flow.kid: Sit by a window. Close your eyes. Listen for sounds that come again and again.
flow.parent: There is always something: a wall clock, a ceiling fan, a dripping tap, a pressure cooker, a crow, a vendor's call, a pigeon. In the morning or evening you may hear a barbet or a koel.

chart.title: One family's list (yours will be your own)

flow.context: This is the first step of Who Else Makes Patterns?, where you listen for repeating sounds from your window. Here you listen.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks one sound from the list. 2. Your child writes it with marks: a dot for a short sound, a line for a long one. 3. Your child loops the part that repeats.
flow.say: Pick one sound. Write it with dots and lines. Then loop the part that repeats.
flow.kid: Pick one sound. Write it with dots and lines. Loop the part that repeats.

chart.title: A cooker written with marks: short wait, long whistle

flow.context: This is step 2 of Who Else Makes Patterns?, where you listen for repeating sounds from your window. Here you write one sound pattern down.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child about the coppersmith barbet, a small green bird with a red forehead. 2. The barbet calls tuk, tuk, tuk at a steady speed, about two tuks each second. 3. Tap that speed on the floor together for ten seconds. 4. Ask what the part that repeats is.
flow.say: A bird called the coppersmith barbet calls tuk, tuk, tuk. Tap it with me. What is the part that repeats?
flow.kid: A barbet calls tuk, tuk, tuk. Tap it: two taps each second. What part repeats?

ask.q: What is the part that repeats in tuk, tuk, tuk?
good: Just one tuk.
Tuk and then a little gap.

flow.parent: Both answers are good. The part can be one tuk, or a tuk and the short silence after it. One of the videos in this unit plays the real call.

chart.title: Three seconds of a barbet's call

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Else Makes Patterns?, where you listen for repeating sounds from your window. Here you tap the call of a bird, the coppersmith barbet.

games.title: Pattern Train
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game. Each player has a rule card and builds a train of small things that follows the rule, a few pieces at a time. The other players watch for a wrong piece. It builds quick carrying on and quick checking.
rules: You need a dice and three kinds of small things, about 15 of each. For example: rajma for red, buttons for blue and chana for yellow.
Each player takes a rule card and keeps it face up. Everyone agrees which thing stands for which colour.
On your turn, roll the dice. Add that many pieces to your train. Say each piece aloud as you put it down.
Every new piece must follow your rule card. When you reach the end of the card, start the card again.
The other players watch. If someone spots a wrong piece, they say 'Check!'. You take back all the pieces from that turn.
The first train to reach 12 pieces wins. The winner reads the whole train aloud.
Playing alone: can you reach 12 pieces in four rolls with no wrong piece? Check by reading your train aloud against the card.
A harder game: turn your rule card face down after your first turn.

setup.art: Two children at a low table, each with a small card showing coloured circles, three bowls of rajma, buttons and chana between them, and a dice.
setup.caption: 1. Take a rule card. Agree which thing stands for each colour.

setup.art: A dice showing 3 and a child adding three pieces to the end of a row of rajma and buttons that follows red, red, blue.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Add that many pieces, keeping your rule.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the rule cards, or copy them on slips of paper. 2. Put out three bowls of small things. 3. Agree which thing stands for red, for blue and for yellow. 4. Each player takes a rule card. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each of us gets a rule card. Our trains must follow our cards. First to 12 pieces wins.
flow.kid: Take a rule card. Choose a thing for each colour. Your train must follow your card.

chart.title: A train that follows the card red, red, blue

flow.context: This is the first step of Pattern Train, a dice game where you build a row of pieces that follows a rule card. Here you set up.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Roll, add the pieces and say each one aloud. 3. Show what to do when the card ends in the middle of a turn: start the card again.
flow.say: I rolled 4. My card is red, red, blue. So I put red, red, blue, and then red again.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Add that many pieces. Say each one aloud. Follow your card.

check.q: Your card says red, blue, blue. Your train is red, blue, blue, red. You roll 2. Which pieces do you add?
check.why: Blue, blue. The train has just begun a new part with red. The part is red, blue, blue, so two blues come next. Picking 'red, blue' means starting the card again on every turn, without looking at where the train stopped.

flow.parent: The most common slip is to start the card from its beginning on every turn. Ask your child to read the whole train aloud before adding to it.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Pattern Train, a dice game where you build a row of pieces that follows a rule card. Here you practise one turn.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Watch each other's trains. 3. Now and then, ask a player what their next piece will be before they roll.
flow.say: Before you roll, tell me what your next piece will be. How do you know?
flow.kid: Play the game. Watch the other trains. Say 'Check!' if you see a wrong piece.

ask.q: Your train has 9 pieces. What will your 10th piece be?
good: I read my train to the end, then I say the next one on my card.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Pattern Train, a dice game where you build a row of pieces that follows a rule card. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. When a train reaches 12 pieces, the game ends. 2. The winner reads the whole train aloud. 3. Everyone checks it against the card.
flow.say: Read your whole train to us. Does every piece follow your card?
flow.kid: The first train with 12 pieces wins. Read your whole train aloud.
flow.context: This is the last step of Pattern Train, a dice game where you build a row of pieces that follows a rule card. Here you finish and check the winning train.

games.title: Which Card Did I Clap?
games.players: 2 to 4 players: with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a clapping game. Eight cards lie face up. One player secretly picks a card and acts out its claps, stamps and pats. The others listen and find the card. It builds the skill of hearing the part that repeats.
rules: Lay the 8 action cards face up where everyone can see them. A pat means patting your lap with both hands.
One player is the leader. The leader secretly chooses a card and does its actions three times round, without stopping.
The others watch and listen. Then each one points to the card they think it was.
The leader says which card it was. Everyone who pointed to it wins one bean.
Then all the players do that pattern together, two more times round.
If nobody found the card, the leader does it again, more slowly.
Take turns to be the leader. When everyone has led twice, the player with the most beans wins.

setup.art: Eight small cards face up on the floor in two rows, each showing little pictures of hands and feet, with three children sitting round them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 8 cards face up.

setup.art: One child clapping with one foot raised to stamp, while two other children watch and listen with their hands on their knees.
setup.caption: 2. The leader acts out one card, three times round.

setup.art: Two children each pointing at a card on the floor while the leader smiles and nods at one of them.
setup.caption: 3. Point to the card you think it was.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 8 action cards, or copy them on slips of paper. 2. Lay them face up. 3. Practise the three actions together: clap, stamp, pat your lap. 4. Read the rules aloud. Put a small heap of beans nearby for scoring.
flow.say: There are three actions: clap, stamp and pat your lap. Let us try each one.
flow.kid: Lay the 8 cards face up. Practise the actions: clap, stamp, pat your lap.

chart.title: The three actions

flow.context: This is the first step of Which Card Did I Clap?, a game where one player acts out a pattern and the others find its card. Here you set up.

flow.do: 1. Be the leader for a practice round. 2. Secretly choose the card clap, stamp, stamp. 3. Do it three times round at a steady speed. 4. Your child points to a card.
flow.say: Listen and watch. I will do one of these cards three times round. Which card is it?
flow.kid: Watch and listen. The leader acts out one card. Point to the card you think it is.

check.q: You hear clap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, stamp. Which card is it?
check.why: It is clap, stamp, stamp: one clap and then two stamps, again and again. Picking 'clap, clap, stamp' means hearing that one action comes twice, but mixing up which one.

flow.parent: Keep the speed steady and do not pause between rounds. The player has to hear where the part starts again.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Which Card Did I Clap?, a game where one player acts out a pattern and the others find its card. Here you play a practice round.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Take turns to be the leader. 3. After each round, everyone does the pattern together two more times.
flow.say: Your turn to lead. Choose a card in your head. Do it three times round.
flow.kid: Take turns to lead. Do your card three times round. Do not stop in the middle.

ask.q: How did you know which card it was?
good: I heard two stamps together.
It started again after three actions.
I said it in my head.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Which Card Did I Clap?, a game where one player acts out a pattern and the others find its card. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. When everyone has led twice, count the beans. 2. Ask which card was the hardest to find, and why.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which card was the hardest to find? Why?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Which card was the hardest to find?
flow.context: This is the last step of Which Card Did I Clap?, a game where one player acts out a pattern and the others find its card. Here you finish and talk about the hardest card.

projects.title: My Pattern Book: five days, five patterns
projects.context: In this five-day project you make a small book with one new pattern on each page: colours, prints, sounds, a pattern you found and a pattern with a hole in it. On the last day someone else reads the book and says what comes next on every page.
projects.problem: A pattern is good only if someone else can read it and carry it on. Can you make five that work?

materials.item: a stamp pad, or a little watercolour or kumkum paste on a plate, for finger prints
a stapler or a needle and thread, for the grown-up

projects.safety: A grown-up staples or sews the book. Wash hands after printing.

schedule.what: Make the book. Page 1: a colour pattern along the page, with two crayons.
Page 2: a print pattern made with a thumb and a fingertip, for example thumb, thumb, fingertip.
Page 3: make up a clap and stamp pattern. Write it with marks, X for a clap and O for a stamp.
Page 4: copy a pattern you found at home, such as a towel stripe, a tile or a sari border.
Page 5: a pattern with one piece left out. Then someone reads the whole book and says what comes next on every page.

projects.record: The book is the record. Under each pattern, loop the part that repeats and write how long it is.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded in half together and stapled along the fold to make a small book, with crayons beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three sheets in half. A grown-up staples the fold.

setup.art: An open page of the little book with a row of thumb prints and fingertip prints in a repeating pattern, and an inky thumb beside it.
setup.caption: 2. One new pattern on each page, one page a day.

setup.art: A grandmother reading the little book while a child watches, the grandmother's finger on an empty box in a row of coloured squares.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, someone else reads it and says what comes next.

flow.do: 1. Fold three sheets of paper in half together. Staple the fold. 2. Your child writes their name on the cover. 3. On page 1, your child draws a row of circles and colours a pattern with two crayons. 4. Your child loops the part that repeats.
flow.say: This is your pattern book. On page 1, make a colour pattern with two crayons. Keep it going to the edge.
flow.kid: Make a colour pattern on page 1. Use two crayons. Loop the part that repeats.

chart.title: One idea for page 1: yellow, green, green

flow.context: This is day 1 of My Pattern Book, a five-day project where you make one new pattern page each day. Here you make the book and the first page.

flow.do: 1. Day 2: a print pattern with a thumb and a fingertip. 2. Day 3: your child makes up a clap and stamp pattern, and writes it with X and O. 3. Day 4: your child copies a pattern found at home. 4. Each day, your child loops the part that repeats.
flow.say: A new page today. Make your pattern. Then show me the part that repeats.
flow.kid: Each day, make one new pattern page. Loop the part that repeats.

ask.q: How long is the part that repeats on today's page?
good: 3: thumb, thumb, fingertip.

flow.parent: Try to have a different length of part on different pages: 2 long on one day, 3 or 4 long on another.
flow.wait: Do one page on each of the next three days.

chart.title: A day 3 page: X is a clap, O is a stamp

flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of My Pattern Book, a five-day project where you make one new pattern page each day. Here you make a print pattern, a sound pattern and a found pattern.

flow.do: 1. On page 5, your child draws a pattern and leaves one box empty in the middle. 2. Your child shows the book to someone at home. 3. That person says what comes next on each page, and fills the empty box. 4. Your child tells them if they are right.
flow.say: Make a pattern with one piece left out. Then let someone read your book and find the missing piece.
flow.kid: Draw a pattern. Leave one box empty. Ask someone to find the missing piece.

ask.q: Could your reader tell what came next on every page? If not, why not?
good: Yes, because the part came round three times.
Not on page 4. I only drew the part once.

chart.title: A page 5 pattern with one box empty

flow.context: This is day 5 of My Pattern Book, a five-day project where you make one new pattern page each day. Here you make a pattern with a hole in it and test the book on a reader.

challenges.title: Stretch: a bookmark with a part four squares long
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. You colour a bookmark of 12 squares with a repeating pattern, using only two colours. The part that repeats must be exactly 4 squares long. The point is to find out that some parts only look 4 long.
challenges.problem: Design a bookmark of 12 squares in two colours. Its part that repeats must be exactly 4 squares long, and it must fit exactly 3 times.
constraints: The part that repeats must be exactly 4 squares long, not shorter.
The bookmark is 12 squares long, so the part must come exactly 3 times.
materials: a strip of squared paper from a maths notebook, 12 squares long and 2 squares wide (or a strip of plain paper ruled into 12 boxes)
spare squared paper for trying ideas
creative: red, blue, blue, red: the two ends of the part match
red, red, blue, red: the single blue is not at the end
Two bookmarks that are the same pattern, but one starts one square later than the other
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own part, 4 squares long, in your two colours. Colour it 3 times along the strip. Then check that no shorter part makes the same bookmark.

setup.art: A strip of squared paper twelve squares long on a table, with two crayons and a few shorter trial strips beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a strip 12 squares long. Choose two colours.

setup.art: The strip with its first four squares coloured red, red, blue, red and a pencil line after the fourth square.
setup.caption: 2. Colour a part 4 squares long. Then repeat it.

setup.art: A finished bookmark coloured in a repeating pattern, tucked into a storybook with the top showing.
setup.caption: 3. Three parts fill the strip. Use it as a bookmark.

flow.do: 1. Cut a strip of squared paper 12 squares long, and a few spare strips. 2. Read the problem and the three limits aloud. 3. Your child colours the first 4 squares of a spare strip in any way, using both colours. 4. Your child repeats those 4 squares to the end.
flow.say: Colour the first four squares any way you like, with both colours. Then do the same four again, to the end.
flow.kid: Colour 4 squares with two colours. Then colour the same 4 again, to the end.

chart.title: 12 squares hold a part of 4 exactly 3 times

rows.label: one part of 4 squares is shaded

flow.context: This is the first step of the bookmark challenge, where you design a pattern whose part is exactly 4 squares long. Here you try a first idea on a spare strip.

flow.do: 1. On a spare strip, colour red, blue, red, blue, to the end. 2. Ask whether its part is really 4 squares long. 3. Cover all but the first 2 squares. Ask whether those 2 already make the whole strip.
flow.say: Here is a part: red, blue, red, blue. Is it really four squares long? Could a shorter part make the same strip?
flow.kid: Look at red, blue, red, blue. Is the part really 4 long? Could a shorter part do it?

ask.q: Why does red, blue, red, blue break the rule of this challenge?
good: Red, blue already makes it.
It is really 2 long, done twice.

flow.parent: This is the trap in the challenge. Red, blue, red, blue does come again and again, but the smaller part red, blue makes the same strip. People have agreed that the part that repeats means the smallest one.

check.q: A strip goes red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. How long is the part that repeats?
check.why: 2 squares. The smallest part that makes the whole strip is red, blue. Picking 4 squares means choosing a part that is really two smaller parts joined together.

chart.title: Is the part 2 long or 4 long?

flow.context: This is step 2 of the bookmark challenge, where you design a pattern whose part is exactly 4 squares long. Here you test a part that only looks 4 squares long.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds as many different parts as they can that are truly 4 long, with two colours. 2. Your child colours each one on spare squared paper. 3. For each one, check that no shorter part makes the same strip.
flow.say: How many different parts can you find that are truly four long? Colour each one. Check each one.
flow.kid: Find as many parts as you can that are truly 4 long. Colour each one.
flow.parent: There are 12 parts that work. They come in three families: three of one colour and one of the other (4 ways for each colour), and two and two with the same colours side by side (4 ways). Your child does not need to find them all. Finding 4 or 5, and checking each one, is very good.

chart.title: Three parts that work. Can you find more?

flow.context: This is step 3 of the bookmark challenge, where you design a pattern whose part is exactly 4 squares long. Here you hunt for all the parts that work.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses a favourite part and colours the real bookmark, 3 times round. 2. Your child gives it to someone at home. 3. That person says which 4 squares would come next if the strip were longer.
flow.say: Choose your best part. Colour the real bookmark. Then test it on someone.
flow.kid: Choose your best part. Colour the bookmark. Ask someone what the next 4 squares would be.

ask.q: Did your reader find the same part as you? Could they have found a different one?
good: Yes, the same four.
They started from the second square, so their part looked different but made the same strip.

flow.context: This is the last step of the bookmark challenge, where you design a pattern whose part is exactly 4 squares long. Here you make the real bookmark and test it on a reader.
